column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
The article dates Nachtigal's treaty only to 1884; the entry's 5 July 1884 is not repeated. Left out: Julien Amegandjin and the remark that Asrafo Plakoo Mlapa was once considered crown prince.

CONFLICT: the entry says he was prime minister from 1912 until his death in 1919. The article says he was prime minister until 1915, when the Bogd Khan abolished the office, and was then appointed minister of war (also 'Minister of the Army'). The text gives no end date for his premiership and leaves out the 1915 abolition and the war ministry.

The article places Tokhtamysh's raid on Azerbaijan in 1385 and the plunder of Tabriz in 1386; the entry speaks of raids on Azerbaijan and Transoxiana without dates. No conflict. Left out: the ruse at Tana, Metropolitan Cyprian and the Vladimir icon, the defeat of Lithuania around 1383, the later history of the successor khanates.

The entry says they crossed into Asia Minor in 278 BCE; the article gives 281-278 BCE for the attacks on Macedonia and Greece and settlement by the end of the 260s, without a year for the crossing. The text gives no year for the crossing. The entry places them around Gordion; the article does not mention Gordion. Left as it is. Left out: Rübekeil's etymology, Chiomara, the raiding division of the seaboard (Aeolis and Ionia).

The article contradicts itself on the end: its mandate is said to have ended with the reported bankruptcy in December 2003, while its list has the fourth prime minister in office until 3 November 2004 and the entry dates it 2000-2004. The text leaves the end of the mandate out. The article says the prime minister was replaced four times in three years; its list names four prime ministers. The text says it had four prime ministers.
The article does not mention the indemnity the entry names; nothing contradicts it.

The article says the treaty was signed by representatives of the emperor Tự Đức's court; Tự Đức is not named in the text, to avoid a date problem (he is generally given as dying in 1883). Left out: the details of the 1949 ceremony at Saigon-Cholon City Hall.
The article calls the towns Brill and Flushing; the entry says Brielle. Not a conflict.

The article dates the Treaty of Kalisz to 1342; the site's entry for it says 1343. The text names it without a year. The article calls the place Raciążek; the entry's name is Raciąż. The text does not name the place.
SKIPPED: article too thin: under 250 words of substance (empty equipment and rank sections, a list of barracks and present-day commanders); it adds little beyond the description

The entry says the party was founded under Ruben Um Nyobè; the article lists other men at the founding meeting and has Um Nyobè take charge as general secretary in November 1948. The text says only that he took charge then and does not say he was absent from the founding. The article attributes Moumié's poisoning in October 1960 to the French secret service; left out, as the entry already tells his death.
Left out: the present contest over the party's leadership (Hugo Patt, Tracy Taegar-Panton) and the list of leaders after 2020, as present-day matters.
The article says most of the Negro Factories Corporation's businesses closed by 1922 in one place and by the mid-1920s in another; the text gives no date for the closures.
The entry says the province existed until 1937; the article gives no end date for the province. Not repeated.
The article is short and mostly plot; the text keeps to it.

The article contradicts itself: it dates the oldest manuscript to 1835 but later says some scholars note the earliest extant manuscript is of the 18th century. The text follows the entry's dates (1835; an early 18th-century one reported) and leaves the second statement out.

The article places the bunker at Rekum, between Rekum and Farge; the entry says at Farge, so the text says between the two. The article gives 553 identified victims and estimates of up to or more than 6,000 dead; the entry's 'more than a thousand' is consistent.

The entry dates the founding of Monte Albán to around 500 BCE; the article says there is no evidence of it in 600 BCE and gives a population of 5,200 by 400 BCE. The text gives only the population figures. The article calls Mitla a Mixtec centre in the Postclassic, while the entry calls Zaachila and Mitla the leading Zapotec centres after Monte Albán; the text names Mitla only among the centres that asserted autonomy in the Classic.

The article dates the excavation by Christos Tsountas to 1889; the entry says 1888. The text gives no year. The article dates the tomb's pottery to around 1500-1450 BCE and says the Cretan cup perhaps dates to the previous century; the entry dates the cups to about 1500 BCE. The text gives no date for the cups or pottery.

The article calls him commander-in-chief of Moscow from 1780 to 1782; the entry says governor-general. The text says only that he was in charge of Moscow. The article's account of Anna's words is drawn from the novelist Valentin Pikul; left out.

The article calls the 1619-1623 harbour the first artificial harbour of Germany; the entry says one of the oldest. The text does not repeat the claim. Lists of festivals, theatre and notable people left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance: a few dated facts and a list of buildings

The article says Vijaya was Champa's capital from 938; the entry says it was the chief royal centre from around the 11th century, and the article itself says its architecture implies importance only from the 11th or 12th century. The date 938 is left out. The disputed Vietnamese raid of 1069 (Michael Vickery argues it did not target Vijaya) and the two conflicting 15th-century population reports (10,000 or 70,000) are left out.

The article says he abdicated in 1400 to become a religious and returned in 1401, while the entry gives an unbroken reign 1389-1429; the text gives the withdrawal as the Pararaton's account. The article also says Kusumawardhani died a year after her son (so 1400) yet names her as a possible successor in 1429; the text gives only the article's statement that her identity as successor is debated. The article's Pararaton quotations date the Regreg war to Saka 1317 and its renewal to after Saka 1323, which do not match the 1406 the article and entry give; the text gives no year for the outbreak beyond the entry's.
The entry says the dukes of Brabant richly endowed the abbey; the article does not say so but lists ducal burials. Anne of Kiev's burial there is marked disputed in the article and is left out.

The entry says Manco withdrew from Cusco in 1537; the article says he withdrew from Ollantaytambo, thinking it too close to Spanish-held Cusco. The text says only that he withdrew to Vitcos after the battle. The article puts the 1544 murderers at seven Spanish renegades; not repeated beyond the entry.

The article dates Vyachko's offer of half his land and fort to Albert to 1205; the entry says 1207. The text gives no year for it. The entry calls him a prince of the Polotsk dynasty; the article says Henry's chronicle suggests he may have come from a local elite, perhaps a Livonian, who converted to Orthodoxy and became a vassal of Polotsk. Left out. The article says Koknese was taken over by the Order by 1209 and Polotsk's formal sovereignty revoked in 1215; left out for length.
The article's statement that 58 sites were known 'as of 2023' and its notes on present-day mining are left out.

The article gives his birth as 16 September 1539; the entry dates him 1541-1576. The text gives no birth year. The article's line that William Piers 'executed Sir Brian mac Phelim O'Neill for treason' contradicts its own account of the execution at Dublin on Essex's orders; Piers is left out. Penelope's and Dorothy's marriages and the infant Francis left out for length.
The article credits the victory at West-Capelle to John I of Avesnes; the entry to William of Holland, who backed him. The text says only that Guy was defeated there.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little beyond the entry

The entry says the main building was modelled on the Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya; the article says the king's monks studied the copy at Bagan. The text gives the article's account, which is consistent with the entry.

The article says that in 1329 Wenceslaus suddenly changed sides and allied with Władysław I, and that John of Bohemia's invasion forced his homage; the entry says he allied with the Knights and did homage in opposition to Władysław. The text tells the invasion and forced homage without saying which side he was on beforehand. The article dates his birth 1293/97; the entry c. 1293. The text gives no birth year.

The article places the Weser region in central Germany; the entry says north-western Germany. Neither is repeated here. The article spells the historian Henry-Russel Hitchcock (sic); only his surname is used.

The article says the Squadron was an independent command until 1856 and again 1866-1867, and that the station was merged with the Cape of Good Hope Station 1832-1841 and 1857-60; left out as inconsistent with the entry's simple 1808-1867. The article's figure of 1,600 ships is given as 'between 1807 and 1860'; the entry has it already, not repeated.

The article says Sant Martí del Canigó was founded in 1007 and consecrated in 1009; the entry gives only the consecration, so the founding year is not repeated. The article lists both 'Raymond (1035-1068), successor in Cerdanya' and 'William I, Count of Cerdanya'; only Raymond is named here.
Nothing is known of his death, so the last section is headed Legacy and covers his workshop only. Some scholars think parts of his sculpture belonged to liturgical furnishings rather than the facade.

The article dates his elevation to duke to 1356-57; the entry says 1356, so the elevation's date is not repeated. The article says he switched to Charles IV after 'the death of his brother-in-law' without saying which; kept as it stands.

The article places his meeting with Luther at 'the Diet of Augsburg in 1521'; the 1521 diet was held at Worms, so the place is left out and only the year kept. The article claims Anhalt-Köthen and Anhalt-Bernburg were the second and third states in the world to adopt Protestantism officially; softened to 'after the Electorate of Saxony'.
The article gives his consecration as 3 August 805 'or perhaps in October or later in 805'; kept hedged.
The article mixes 'Nanking' and 'Nanjing'; Nanjing used throughout. Its month-first dates are turned day-first.

The entry says he died after a boating accident; the article does not mention this, so the cause of death is not given here. The article gives his birth as c. October 501 in the lead and 'winter 501' in the text; 'the winter of 501' used.
The entry says he entered office in his forties; the article gives only 359 for his return, which fits; no age stated here.

The entry says Lunda warriors conquered the Yaka in the 18th century; the article says Kabamba led the exodus around the 17th century and founded the kingdom then, while 'other sources' give the Lunda Empire's expansion in the 1730s. No date is given here. The entry calls the kings kiamfu; the article calls the paramount chief kiambv. Neither title is used here. The article is poorly written in places; the names of individual kings (Kabamba Faustin, Tsiimba Nkumbi, Koko Kodia Puanga) are left out because the article's account of them is confused.

The entry dates his death to 938; the article gives 21 January 939 ('around new year 939'). No year is given here. The article's lead says he yielded the throne in 938, its text in winter 937; the entry says 937. The abdication's year is not repeated here.
Only the lead and section openings were available; the struggle with Sun Ru for Huainan in the 890s is only partly given and is left out.

The entry calls it the winter capital of the Oghuz yabghu; the article says only capital. 'Winter' is not repeated or contradicted. The article gives the Oghuz polity's destruction by the Kipchaks and Kimeks in the 12th century; left out as it concerns the polity, not the town.
The article gives his birth as 1883; the entry has c. 1883. No birth year is stated here. The article does not say where he died, so no place of death is given.
The article dates his death to 22 March 619 in the lead; the entry gives 619 only; no day used.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words and the entry already gives most of it: his vassalage to Alfonso VII, the exchange of Rueda and his death near Chinchilla in 1146

The article lists Yuan Zuguang as a zaju playwright whose plays 'reflected elements of the Wuxu Reform' (1898); left out as doubtful. The entry names historical, romantic and moral themes; the article stresses comedy and happy endings; not contradicted.

The entry attributes the story to Ctesias's Persica and later writers such as Diodorus and calls it semi-legendary; the article names only Diodorus Siculus and gives Schmitt (legendary) and Mayor (historical). Neither source attribution is repeated here; the scholars' views are given as the article gives them. Diodorus names the Median king Astibaras; the article identifies him with Cyaxares. Left unnamed.
The 27,000 km2 figure is the article's own; the Shiji figure is 40,000 qing. Both given as the article gives them.
Left out the article's claim that 'Zidan and his forces invaded the Songhai Empire in 1593', ten years before his reign; it is doubtful as worded.
Short article; two sections only. The entry spells the ruler Jaafar Nimeiry, the article Gaafar Nimeiry: same person.
Article gives the reign as 949-961 without 'c.'; the entry has 'c. 949'. No conflict in the text.
Article: ruled Gandhara and possibly most of the Indus region c. 46-60; entry says Punjab and Gandhara. Not stated against the entry.

Entry speaks of naval warfare against Aragon and Sicily; the article names only Portuguese fleets. Not a contradiction, both kept as they are. Article text for Morocco is garbled ('pake marinid vassal of Tunis'), read as making the Marinid ruler a vassal.

The entry says he wrote the life of Henry II; the article says the Vita Heinrici II imperatoris 'has been ascribed to him, but the evidence ... is not decisive'. Left the Vita out of the text. The entry's cathedral consecration in 1023 is not in the article. 'church historian' for Hauck is my gloss; article gives only 'Hauck'.

Article says the Addizione 'more than doubled' the walled town; entry says 'roughly doubled'. Left the size out. Article spells the street 'Biagio Rosetti' once; used the architect's spelling Rossetti.

Article's chronology of the Enzo marriage is unclear (Ubaldo's will dated January 1237, Enzo arriving 'in October the same year as Ubaldo's death'); the entry gives 1238. Left the year of the marriage out of the text.
Kept 'High King 862-879' consistent with the article's 17-year reign. Order of his marriages uncertain in the article; only Land and Máel Muire named.

Article places the historical kingdom between the Pra and Ankobra rivers; the entry says between the Ankobra River and Takoradi. Left the extent out. The article says the Butre pact 'lasted for 213 years until 1871', which does not add up from 1656; gave only the end year. Entry's Brandenburg fort and Busua as capital are not in the article. Article is of poor quality and editorial; kept to its plain facts.

Article gives Addo Dankwa III's reign as 'over thirty years' and 'over 40 years'; left the length out. Article calls the Abiriw dispute '20-year-old' in 2013 although it dates the clash to 2002-2003; left the length out. Entry's Basel Mission dates (1835, seminary 1848) are not in the article.

Article spells Khwarezemids/Khwarezmids variously; used Khwarezemids as the entry does (entry: Khwarazmians). The article's account of La Forbie is confused (says he left to fight the Khwarezemids and was overwhelmed at La Forbie); kept to the outcome.
SKIPPED: article of about 280 words; beyond the entry it adds only his father's career and a few lines on the reign, not enough for 260 words without padding

Article calls Bejaia first a 'second capital' and then 'his capital'; the entry calls it a new capital. Left the capital status out of the text. The name al-Nasiriyya is in the entry, not the article.

The entry dates the complex mainly to the late 11th to early 13th centuries; the article says the structures date from the early 12th to early 13th centuries and that the inscriptions date the Dukhang no earlier than 1140, and elsewhere mentions a royal inscription dated c. 1200. Left the founding date out of the text; gave only the Sumtseg (early 13th century) and Manjushri Temple (c. 1225) dates, which fall inside the entry's range.

The article's lead also says he commanded French forces in the second expeditionary force against the Boxer Rebellion and in the First Franco-Dahomean War; the body does not tell either, so both are left out. The article's racial term 'quadroon' is not used.

The article says excavations found a castle on the site already in the 12th century; the entry says the residence was built from the mid-13th century. Left out to avoid an apparent contradiction. Left out: the 2005/2006 redevelopment into offices and apartments, and Hitler's 1914 painting of the courtyard.

The article dates his contention for the throne to 1497-1504/5; the entry gives his death as 1504. The end date is left out of the text. The article's sentence about a letter asking to return to Shah Ismail's service is unclear as to who wrote it; left out.
The article gives his rule as 360 to c. 351 BC; the entry gives fl. 359-351 BCE. The start year is left out of the text.
The article says he was appointed susuhunan in 1645 and crowned in 1646; the entry gives his reign from 1646. The 1645 date is left out.
The lead says he 'explored and discovered for France Saharan Africa'; left out as vague.

The article contradicts itself on his reign: the lead gives 814-878, the body says he ascended in 815 and reigned 815-877, retiring in 877. The entry gives 814-878; no year of accession or retirement is printed. The article also links the Prashnottara Ratnamalika to Gunabhadra in one place and to Vimalacharya in another.
The article gives his death as 10 April 759, consistent with the entry; the day is omitted only for length. Huige is the article's name for the Uyghurs of the entry.

The article says he ruled from 1078 until his death in 1150, 72 years according to his own inscription; the entry gives r. 1078-1147. No end date or length is printed. The article calls him both the founder of the Eastern Ganga dynasty and the son of an Eastern Ganga king; the founder claim is left out.

The article spells the name Potti Sreeramulu; the entry Potti Sriramulu. The article spelling is used in the text. The article dates Sreeramulu's death to midnight of 15 December, i.e. early 16 December 1952; printed as the early hours of 16 December. Left out: the Hyderabad leaders' claims about Communist support for the merger.
The article dates him fl. 1540-1575; consistent with the entry's 'mid-sixteenth century'.

The article gives 77 years of civil war after his death; the entry says 'nearly a century of rivalry'. No figure is printed. The article gives his dates as 1675-1710 without 'c.'; the entry hedges 'c. 1675'. His accession year 1675 is printed as the article gives it.

The entry names the air bases as Habbaniyah and Shaibah; the article (quoting Churchill) says near Basra and Habbaniya. Both can be true (Shaibah is near Basra) but the article does not name Shaibah; the text follows the article's wording without contradicting the entry.
The entry calls his son Ferry; the article Frederick (Ferry is the French form). The text uses Frederick. Thin article: family list used for the third section.

The article gives her dates as c. 1153 - c. 1188 (her parents married around 1153 and she was at most seventeen in 1170); the entry gives c. 1145-1188. No birth year or age is printed. The article calls her year of death unclear, 1188 being one suggestion; the entry gives 1188. No year of death is printed in the text.

The article gives the move to the Almogàvers building as 1994 in the lead and as from 1993 in the body; the text gives no year. It also says the archive was in the palace from 1318, though it calls the palace sixteenth-century; the text avoids both. The article says the Liber feudorum maior holds documents from the 9th century, consistent with the entry.

The entry calls him an Athenian philosopher; the article's biography (from Posidonius via Athenaeus) may in part belong to Athenion. The text attributes it as 'the account that has come down'. The article says he was executed by poison; the entry says 'put to death', consistent.
The article estimates completion in 1030 but also writes 'assuming that is between 1028 and 1035'; only the entry's date is used (not repeated).

The entry says Hideyoshi's wife Nene had been adopted into the family; the article says the sister of Asano Nagamasa married Hideyoshi. The text follows the article without naming Nene; the two may describe the same tie. The article gives conflicting dates: Nagamasa 1546-1611 in the branch list but 1526-1610 under significant members; Naganori 1667-1701 and 1647-1701. No birth years are printed. The article does not give the years 1619 and 1871 of the entry.
The entry says 'traditionally at an assembly in Ariano in 1140'; the article states the summer of 1140 at Ariano without hedging. Consistent.

The article gives his death as 285 or 284 BCE; the entry says 285. It also dates the Bosporan and Paeonian grain gift to the spring of 284, which cannot stand with a death in 285. I gave neither the death year nor the date of the gift. The entry describes his silver coins as showing Apollo and a horseman; the article speaks of Athena heads and later Alexander-type tetradrachms. I gave the article's account of the change of type without contradicting the entry's description of other issues. The article spells the father Patraus, the entry Patraos; I left the name out. The article misspells Demetrius's epithet (Poliocretes), so I left the epithet out.
The entry dates the building to the 15th or 16th century; the article says the late 15th century, around 1490, which falls within the entry's range.

The article says the revolt lasted three years from 1239; the entry dates it 1239-1240. I gave no duration. Baba Ishak is spelled Ishaq in the entry; I used the article's spelling Ishak, which the checks require. The article calls the hired troops mercenaries of French origin; the entry says Frankish mercenaries.

The article says the Feyli Kurds migrated in the 19th century under Safavid Iran, which is an anachronism (the Safavids fell in the 18th century); I gave the century only. Left out the oilfield's projected capacity for 2017 and the hydrogeological figures, which are given in garbled units.
Thin article; written close to its limit.
The article dates Emery's excavations to 1928-1931; the entry says 'in the 1930s'. I gave no years for the excavation. The article says 'Nasser Lake'; I wrote Lake Nasser as the entry does.

The Ekalinga Mahatmya also gives his abdication as 753 or 764 CE; left out as the entry gives only the 8th century. Entry says tradition has him take Chittor from its Mori rulers; the article's scholars mostly say the Arabs defeated the Moris and Bappa then took Chittor after repulsing the Arabs, while Mishra has him succeed the Mori ruler. I gave the scholars' views attributed, without stating the tradition in a form that conflicts.

The entry dates Bargal's role as a residence of the boqors to the 19th and early 20th centuries; the article says it may have been founded in the early modern period as a seasonal headquarters. Not in conflict, but I kept the article's hedge. The article does not say who bombed Bargal in October 1925; the entry speaks of the Italian conquest in the 1920s. I did not name the attacker.

The article says Barisone himself was held in Genoa and not allowed to return until 1168, and also that his wife and brother-in-law were hostages until 1171 when 'Barisone and his family were freed'. I followed the order of events without claiming he was held after 1168. The article names the ruler of Torres, to whose court Peter fled, also Barisone II; I left that out to avoid confusion.

The article both says the fort was built by Harihara I and that there are remains of two forts built by the Alupas and the Vijayanagara governors; I gave both, the first as an attribution. The article's statement that a Ganapathy temple was built '900 years back, during the Chola Period' is left out as undated and doubtful.

The entry says the legion lost its eagle; the article's lead says the aquila was captured but its battle section says Suetonius 'possibly in error' mentions the loss. I left the eagle out. Casualty figures (5,300 infantry and 480 cavalry) agree with the entry's 'nearly 6,000'.

The article dates the final cession to 13 August 1814 and the Congress of Vienna to 1814; consistent with the entry. Where the final articles were signed is uncertain (Goedeverwachting estate or Gerhard Croeser's farm); left out.

The entry says Lucullus won 'after cutting the enemy supply lines'; the article describes Pontic attacks on Lucullus's own supply convoys, which failed. I told the convoy fights as the article does without repeating or denying the entry's phrase.
Article spells the American eyewitness T.H. Nelson.
The entry says the city of Bern surrendered on the day of the battle (5 March); the article says the government of Bern had surrendered the previous day (4 March). I gave no date for the surrender.
Kilometres used as in the article's conversion (60 miles, 97 km).

The article's lead names the Afghan commander as Wazir Akbar Khan, the entry speaks of an army sent by Dost Mohammad Khan; both consistent. Article uses both Nalwa and Nawla; I used Nalwa as the entry does. Christine Noelle's view that Dost Mohammad had no real ambition to take Peshawar in 1837 left out for length.

The article calls the city Cuzco; the entry writes Cusco. The article's lead says the forces of Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro; the entry says Francisco's forces led by Hernando: both kept compatible. Nothing said of the aftermath beyond the article's points (execution already in the entry).

The article says Palmares controlled large areas 'during the Dutch-Portuguese War', which does not fit its own dating of the enslavement after 1665; left out. Battle date 29 October 1665 in the article; not stated, entry gives only 1665 (no conflict).

The article calls Sveinn a 'Swedish vassal' governing a Swedish part of Norway; the entry says he ruled under Danish overlordship. Left the overlordship out. The article also says 'Danish rule folded' after Eirikr left; worded as the brothers' power weakening.

The article says about one-third of the Egyptian soldiers surrendered and were later freed; the entry says few survivors. Left the surrender figure out. The article's 'fuzzy-wuzzies' nickname omitted.
Casualty figures: article gives 6,800 Serbian vs 2,300 Bulgarian, and Serbian sources 3,000 vs 2,500 for the battle and 7,000 vs 5,000 for the war; only the first given, the second acknowledged.
The article says the Swiss in the garden were killed 'to the last man'; the entry says the force was 'almost entirely destroyed'. Worded without 'to the last man'.

The article also says the victory consolidated Chilean control of Tarapacá, annexed under the Treaty of Ancón of 20 October 1883. The article spells the colonel Velasquez and Velázquez; used Velasquez.
Sallust's narrative is the source for the battle's detail. The article says 'Metellus' defeat at Zama'; worded as 'checked at Zama'.

The article names the battle Kountouras (owner's name, variant Koundouron); used no spelling of the grove in the text. Frankish numbers (Chronicle 700, elder Villehardouin little above 500 mounted) left out: the entry already summarises them as a few hundred. The two sources also place the battle after Kalamata or after Modon.
The entry credits Zhang Liao's vanguard with the rout and the killing of Tadun; the article says Zhang Liao led the offensive and Cao Chun's brigade captured Tadun. Compatible as written.
Folklore of a wooden statue of Zhuge Liang left out. Jiang Wan named as successor 'took the chancellor's post' per article.

SKIPPED: article has about 250 words of substance, and its main addition (Baz Bahadur regained Malwa after 1561 and lost it finally in 1562; reign 1555-1562) conflicts with the entry's reign dates of 1555-1561 Article: reigned 1555 to 1562; defeated at Sarangpur 29 March 1561; regained the kingdom briefly with Khandesh and Berar; defeated by Abdullah Khan in 1562; surrendered to Akbar at Agra in November 1570. Entry: r. 1555-1561. The entry's dates may need correcting to 1562.
The surgeon's diary quoted by Elspeth Huxley omitted. The article says the British freed about 100 enslaved carriers and later instituted forced labour; not included for length.

The article dates the first mentions confusingly: a document of 1020 naming Otto von Northeim, the Werden Abbey registers of 1050, and Gertrud named comitissa de Benetheim in 1050 though placed after 1116. The entry says first recorded in the late 11th or early 12th century. All first-mention dates left out.

The article calls Harsha 'of Thaneswar'; the entry 'of Kannauj': no place given in the text for Harsha. Karnasuvarna appears in the article only as a copper plate grant; the entry's capture of it not repeated. The article's 'restored Varman rule' and 'last ruler of the Varman dynasty' kept.

The entry says the revolt was put down by Kim Yu-sin and Kim Chunchu; the article says Kim Yushin and Kim Alcheon. Only Kim Yushin named as the commander against him. Article variants (Pidam dying mid-revolt, Seondeok dying two days in) omitted. Spelling: article Pidam / Kim Yushin; entry Bidam / Kim Yu-sin.
Article is short (about 400 words); text kept to what it gives.

The article says Sue pottery 'from the Heian period in the 6th century' and Bizen appearing 'during the Kamakura period of the 14th century': both centuries look wrong for the periods, so no centuries given. The Imbe clay is called both Imbe and Inbe.
The article's lead says the brothers were installed 'on his father's death in 1063', which its own Background does not support (Cynfyn 'first appears' in 1063); left out.
The article says the revolution was in alliance with liberals and communists; not repeated. Inflation figures (190 to 15,000 pesos per dollar) left out for length.

The article gives the smaller monuments as 21 smaller burial mounds in its lead and 25 smaller cairns in its Background section; the count is left out. The 2019 find is reported as 'believed to be' a ship burial; hedged accordingly.

Champollion's reading Ioudahamalek corresponds in the modern list to no. 29, read Yad Hammelek, 'hand of the king'; the article does not say so explicitly, so the text gives only Champollion's reading as his.

The article says the family spans the 7th to 9th centuries, but its own list ends with Jibrail III, who died in 1006; the span is not restated. The tradition that a member treated Ali ibn Husayn Zayn al-Abidin at Karbala ('it is even said') is left out as doubtful.

The article gives two contradicting dates for Peter's visit and wedding: Peter arrived in Constantinople in November 927, yet married Irene on 8 October 927. Both are left out. The bride is Irene Lekapene in the lead and Maria Lekapene, renamed Irene, in the treaty section; the text gives the latter, which reconciles both. The annexation of Serbia at the end of 924 is left out for length.
The article spells the Roman base both Agedincum and Agendicum; Agedincum is used throughout.

The article says the site was destroyed by fire 'no later than 370 BCE'; the entry dates the building to the 6th–late 5th century BCE. The date of the destruction is left out. The entry's Greek pottery, jewellery and weapons are not in the article.
